newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan chip shares unaffected by book-to-bill rise.
newsitem.headline: Japan chip shares unaffected by book-to-bill rise.

text.p: Shares in Japanese chip makers showed little reaction to news that the industry's key indicator -- the North American book-to-bill ratio -- rose in September to its highest level this year, traders said on Wednesday.
In Tokyo morning trading, shares in Fujitsu Ltd were 10 yen lower at 1,040 yen, while NEC Corp shares were unchanged at 1,260 yen.
Shares in Mitsubishi Electric Corp slipped by one yen to 725 yen and those in Toshiba Corp fell four yen to 749 yen. Hitachi Ltd shares were flat at 1,050 yen.

On Tuesday, the Semiconductor Industry Association said the North American book-to-bill ratio, which measures the value of orders against shipments, rose to 0.99 in September from a revised 0.93 in August. The ratio means manufacturers received $99 in new orders last month for every $100 in shipments.
Industry analysts expected the ratio to inch closer to the breakeven level with most estimates averaging around 0.95.

But the market here showed a muted reaction. "The atmosphere is too subdued, with no reason whatsoever to buy stocks, and that is nullifying the fairly strong book-to-bill ratio," Sanyo Securities strategist Keiji Arai said.

The ratio, a leading indicator of future demand tallied by the industry's trade group, has been improving recently, reflecting an increase in orders by personal computer makers and more stable prices for memory chips.

Prices of dynamic random access memory chips, or DRAMs, had plummeted during the year to a fraction of what they were in January. But since mid-September, memory prices have risen 30 to 50 percent from their lows.
"The figure is almost in line with what was estimated and that shows that the semiconductor business is in a recovery trend," said Hiroyuki Iba, a Nikko Research Centre analyst.

"Orders for chips for the Christmas shopping period started to appear in the latter half of September. And orders would be expected to rise in October and in the first half of November, although a strong recovery may be difficult. When the bottom (of business) is confirmed and the recovery becomes clear, the (chip) sector should attract more attention," Nikko's Iba said.
Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd said in its latest commentary that the recovery in the book-to-bill ratio this time was largely due to seasonal factors.
"We are revising our stance towards the semiconductor sector only from cautious to neutral," it said.

Salomon Brothers said personal computer manufacturers resumed ordering parts in September, as they expected demand for the Christmas season and have reduced their inventories to the lowest levels possible.

"As the effect of inventory adjustments conducted by DRAM manufacturers from this summer will linger for the next two to three months, DRAM prices may remain at the current level and and the BB ratio may surpass 1.0," it said.

It also warned against yet another possible decline in DRAM prices early next year, but added that in the fiscal year starting April 1997, the supply and demand balance could vary greatly, depending on the trend in suppliers' capital investment.

"It is possible that South Korean manufacturers will take a gamble and try to seize dominance of the DRAM market from the Japanese manufacturers, but this is an unpredictable factor," Salomon said in its commentary.

On Tuesday, Fujitsu said it planned to boost output of next-generation 64-megabit memories to meet growing demand for the higher capacity chips. But other Japanese makers said they had no immediate plans to follow suit, signalling caution about switching to the newer type of chip despite a recent fall in prices for the current mainstay memory chips. -- Tokyo Equities Desk (3-81-3432-9052)
